As indicated earlier in this Provisional Findings, the TCCC is alleged to have

I../

in the relevant market fits a theory of harm of priq\e\disfcrimination.

Price discrimination is a term that econorfusts\''use to describe the practice of
•r--
selling the same product to different cus_t6mers at different prices even though
the cost of sale is the same. More,pre9i§`ely, it is se[[ing at a price or prices such
that the ratio of price to margi<n?i\6o\sts is different in different sales3.
Other literature defines pri'`?e,`discrimination in markets for tangible products and
(, y/y``,
services as selling th6'' sa"me product to different customers for different prices
when those differ6n\`6es are not justified by differences in costs.
Several case` laws have established that, price discrimination may be
exploitative of customers, for example, where higher prices are charged to
"locked in" customers unable to switch to alternative suppliers; it can also be
ha-rmful to the competitive process, where it leads to a distortion of competition
in the markets downstream of the dominant undertaking. The case law
establishes that, in determining whether there is discrimination in the form of the
application of dissimilar conditions to equivalent transactions with other trading
parties, thereby placing the discriminated party at a competitive disadvantage,
five issues must be addressed:
